claim: Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, which require ownership of mobile phones, are being investigated throughout Africa.
source: Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, which require ownership of mobile phones, are being investigated throughout Africa.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies investigating mHealth interventions in Africa

claim: The study analyzed data from 44,224 individuals in 33 African countries from Round 7 of the Afrobarometer surveys conducted in 2017-2018.
source: We use nationally representative data collected in 2017–2018 from 44,224 individuals in Round 7 of the Afrobarometer surveys.
evidence: Direct statement of the data source and sample size used in the study

claim: 82% of individuals in 33 African countries own mobile phones.
source: We find 82% of individuals in 33 countries own mobile phones: 42% BPs and 40% SPs.
evidence: Quantitative finding from analysis of Afrobarometer survey data

claim: 42% of individuals in 33 African countries own basic phones (BPs).
source: We find 82% of individuals in 33 countries own mobile phones: 42% BPs and 40% SPs.
evidence: Quantitative finding from analysis of survey data

claim: 40% of individuals in 33 African countries own smartphones (SPs).
source: We find 82% of individuals in 33 countries own mobile phones: 42% BPs and 40% SPs.
evidence: Quantitative finding from analysis of survey data

claim: Individuals who live close to a health clinic have higher odds of mobile phone ownership than those who do not (aOR: 1.31, 95% HPD region: 1.24–1.39).
source: Individuals who live close to an HC have higher odds of ownership than those who do not (aOR: 1.31, Bayesian 95% highest posterior density [HPD] region: 1.24–1.39).
evidence: Statistical result from Bayesian multilevel logistic regression model

claim: Men have over twice the odds of mobile phone ownership compared with women (aOR: 2.37, 95% HPD region: 1.96–2.84).
source: Men, compared with women, have over twice the odds of ownership (aOR: 2.37, 95% HPD region: 1.96–2.84).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis

claim: Urban residents have almost three times the odds of mobile phone ownership compared with rural residents (aOR: 2.66, 95% HPD region: 2.22–3.18).
source: Urban residents, compared with rural residents, have almost three times the odds (aOR: 2.66, 95% HPD region: 2.22–3.18)
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis

claim: Among mobile phone owners, urban residents have nearly three times the odds of owning a smartphone compared to rural residents (aOR: 2.67, 95% HPD region: 2.33–3.10).
source: amongst mobile phone owners, nearly three times the odds of owning an SP (aOR: 2.67, 95% HPD region: 2.33–3.10).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis

claim: Mobile phone ownership increases with age, peaks in 26–40 year olds, then decreases.
source: Ownership increases with age, peaks in 26–40 year olds, then decreases.
evidence: Pattern observed in the data analysis

claim: Individuals under 30 are more likely to own a smartphone than a basic phone.
source: Individuals under 30 are more likely to own an SP than a BP
evidence: Pattern observed in age-stratified analysis

claim: Older individuals are more likely to own a basic phone than a smartphone.
source: older individuals more likely to own a BP than an SP.
evidence: Pattern observed in age-stratified analysis

claim: Probability of mobile phone ownership decreases with the Lived Poverty Index.
source: Probability of ownership decreases with the Lived Poverty Index
evidence: Pattern observed in the data analysis

claim: Some of the poorest individuals own smartphones.
source: however, some of the poorest individuals own SPs.
evidence: Observation from the data analysis

claim: Rolling out mHealth interventions in Africa is likely to propagate already existing inequities in access to healthcare if digital devices are not equally available within the population.
source: If the digital devices needed for mHealth interventions are not equally available within the population (which we have found is the current situation), rolling out mHealth interventions in Africa is likely to propagate already existing inequities in access to healthcare.
evidence: Inference drawn from the findings about inequities in mobile phone ownership

claim: The 33 countries analyzed encompass approximately 60% of the population of the African continent.
source: together, these 33 countries encompass ~60% of the population of the African continent, which contains ~1.4 billion people.
evidence: Statement about the representativeness of the sample

claim: The African continent contains approximately 1.4 billion people.
source: which contains ~1.4 billion people.
evidence: Statement of demographic fact

claim: Afrobarometer is a pan-African, non-partisan research project that has been operating since 1999.
source: Afrobarometer is a pan-African, non-partisan research project that has been operating since 1999.
evidence: Description of the data source

claim: Afrobarometer is the world's leading source of high-quality public opinion data for Africa.
source: It is the world's leading source of high-quality public opinion data for Africa.
evidence: Statement about the reputation of the data source

claim: The phenomenon of distance decay in utilization of health clinics has been observed in many African countries.
source: The phenomenon of distance decay in utilization of HCs has been observed in many African countries: the further individuals live from an HC, the less likely they are to utilize healthcare (Lankowski et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: Geographic inaccessibility of health clinics has been associated with decreased utilization of antenatal care and bed nets, lower vaccination rates, higher attrition rates from HIV and tuberculosis treatment programs, lower adherence levels in HIV programs, reduced maternal fever-seeking behavior, and uptake in contraception.
source: The geographic inaccessibility of HCs has been shown to be associated with decreased utilization of antenatal care and bed nets (for protection against malaria), lower vaccination rates, higher attrition rates from HIV and tuberculosis treatment programs, lower adherence levels in HIV programs, reduced maternal fever-seeking behavior, and uptake in contraception (Alegana et al., 2018; Bilinski et al., 2017; Ouma et al., 2017; Terzian et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: Multiple mHealth interventions are being investigated or used at a small scale in almost every African country.
source: Currently, there are multiple mHealth interventions that are being investigated or being used at a small scale in almost every African country (Holst et al., 2020; Manby et al., 2022; Onukwugha et al., 2022; Osei et al., 2021; Wood et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies

claim: Throughout Africa, mHealth interventions are being used for disease diagnosis and treatment support by health workers.
source: Throughout the continent, mHealth interventions are being used for multiple reasons: for disease diagnosis and treatment support by health workers (Anstey Watkins et al., 2018; Wood et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being used to increase adolescents' use of sexual and reproductive health services.
source: to increase adolescents' use of sexual and reproductive health services (Onukwugha et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being used for HIV prevention and management.
source: for HIV prevention and management (Manby et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being used to improve maternal and child health.
source: to improve maternal and child health (Ag Ahmed et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being used to support the COVID-19 response.
source: to support the COVID-19 response (Fischer et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being used to improve surveillance coverage for new outbreaks of infectious diseases such as Ebola.
source: and to improve surveillance coverage for new outbreaks of infectious diseases (e.g. Ebola; Tom-Aba et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research

claim: Kenya was excluded from the analysis because its questionnaire did not differentiate between smartphone and basic phone ownership.
source: We excluded Kenya from our analysis as its questionnaire did not differentiate between SP and BP ownership.
evidence: Methodological decision explained in the text

claim: Only 13% of individuals classified as smartphone owners reported that they never accessed the internet.
source: Notably, we found that only 13% of individuals that we classified as SP owners (and 89% of individuals that we classified as owners of BP) reported that they never accessed the internet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: 89% of individuals classified as basic phone owners reported that they never accessed the internet.
source: Notably, we found that only 13% of individuals that we classified as SP owners (and 89% of individuals that we classified as owners of BP) reported that they never accessed the internet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: The probability of not owning a mobile phone has a median of 0.15 across the 33 countries.
source: Overall, the probability of not owning a mobile phone (either a BP or an SP) is fairly low (median: 0.15), but there is substantial variation between countries: the probability ranges from 0.05 to 0.53 with SD 0.12.
evidence: Statistical summary of the data

claim: The probability of not owning a mobile phone ranges from 0.05 to 0.53 across the 33 countries with a standard deviation of 0.12.
source: the probability ranges from 0.05 to 0.53 with SD 0.12.
evidence: Statistical summary of the data

claim: The probability of owning a basic phone has a median of 0.40 across the 33 countries.
source: The probability of owning a BP is moderately high (median: 0.40), but again – there is substantial variation amongst countries, ranging from 0.23 to 0.66 with SD 0.10.
evidence: Statistical summary of the data

claim: The probability of owning a basic phone ranges from 0.23 to 0.66 across the 33 countries with a standard deviation of 0.10.
source: ranging from 0.23 to 0.66 with SD 0.10.
evidence: Statistical summary of the data

claim: The country-level probability of owning a basic phone is not significantly different from the probability of owning a smartphone (t=0.76; p=0.45).
source: Overall, the country-level probability of owning a BP is not significantly different (t=0.76; p=0.45) from the probability of owning an SP
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: The probability of owning a smartphone is much more variable amongst countries (SD=0.16) than basic phone ownership.
source: but the probability of owning an SP is much more variable amongst countries (SD=0.16).
evidence: Statistical comparison of variability

claim: There is substantial sub-national variation within almost every one of the 33 countries in the ownership of basic phones and smartphones.
source: Notably, there is substantial sub-national variation, within almost every one of the 33 countries, in the ownership of a BP (Figure 1C) or of an SP (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observation from geographic analysis shown in figures

claim: Smartphone owners were more likely than basic phone owners to live close to a health clinic (t=6.86; p<0.001).
source: SP owners were more likely than BP owners to live close to an HC (t=6.86; p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: Basic phone owners were significantly more likely than individuals who did not own a mobile phone to live close to a health clinic (t=5.52; p<0.001).
source: in turn, BP owners were significantly more likely than individuals who did not own a mobile phone to live close to an HC (t=5.52; p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: 87% of men versus 76% of women own mobile phones across the 33 countries.
source: Considering the 33 countries together, we found a gender inequity in ownership of mobile phones: 87% of men versus 76% of women own mobile phones.
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis

claim: 50% of men who own mobile phones own smartphones versus 46% of women who own mobile phones.
source: We also found a gender inequity in ownership of SPs: 50% of men (who own mobile phones) own SPs versus 46% of women (who own mobile phones).
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis

claim: Men are significantly more likely than women to own mobile phones in 27 out of the 33 countries.
source: We found that men are significantly more likely than women to own mobile phones in 27 out of the 33 countries (Table 1)
evidence: Summary of country-specific analyses shown in table

claim: The odds ratio of male to female phone ownership is greatest in Benin (cOR 4.78).
source: the OR of male to female phone ownership is greatest in Benin (cOR 4.78).
evidence: Quantitative finding from country-specific analysis

claim: No significant gender difference in mobile phone ownership was found in Botswana, Cabo Verde, Gabon, Lesotho, Namibia, or South Africa.
source: We did not find a significant gender difference in Botswana, Cabo Verde, Gabon, Lesotho, Namibia, or South Africa.
evidence: Summary of country-specific statistical tests

claim: Among mobile phone owners, men are significantly more likely than women to own smartphones in 15 of the 33 countries.
source: Amongst mobile phone owners, men are significantly more likely than women to own SPs in 15 of the 33 countries (Table 1)
evidence: Summary of country-specific analyses shown in table

claim: Gender inequity in smartphone ownership among mobile phone owners is most pronounced in Benin (cOR 2.84).
source: gender inequity is most pronounced in Benin (cOR 2.84).
evidence: Quantitative finding from country-specific analysis

claim: 91% of urban residents versus 74% of rural residents own mobile phones across the 33 countries.
source: Considering the 33 countries together, we found a substantial inequity in ownership of mobile phones based on whether individuals lived in urban or rural areas: 91% of urban residents versus 74% of rural residents.
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis

claim: 61% of urban residents who own mobile phones own smartphones versus 35% of rural residents who own mobile phones.
source: We also found an urban-rural inequity in ownership of SPs: 61% of urban residents (who own mobile phones) own SPs versus 35% of rural residents (who own mobile phones).
evidence: Quantitative finding from data analysis

claim: Significant urban-rural differences in mobile phone ownership were found in 29 of the 33 countries.
source: We found significant urban-rural differences in the ownership of mobile phones in 29 of the 33 countries (Table 2)
evidence: Summary of country-specific analyses shown in table

claim: The odds ratio of urban to rural phone ownership is greatest in Gabon (cOR 7.17).
source: the OR of urban to rural phone ownership is greatest in Gabon (cOR 7.17).
evidence: Quantitative finding from country-specific analysis

claim: No significant urban-rural inequity in mobile phone ownership was found in Eswatini, the Gambia, Mauritius, or South Africa.
source: Notably, we did not find a significant urban-rural inequity in Eswatini, the Gambia, Mauritius, or South Africa.
evidence: Summary of country-specific statistical tests

claim: Urban residents are more likely to own smartphones than rural residents in 31 of 33 countries.
source: Urban residents are more likely to own SPs than rural residents, in 31 of 33 countries (Table 2)
evidence: Summary of country-specific analyses shown in table

claim: The urban/rural difference in smartphone ownership is greatest in Burkina Faso (cOR 7.57).
source: the urban/rural difference in SP ownership is greatest in Burkina Faso (cOR 7.57).
evidence: Quantitative finding from country-specific analysis

claim: No significant urban-rural differences in smartphone ownership were found in the Gambia or Sao Tome and Principe.
source: We did not find significant urban-rural differences in ownership of SPs in the Gambia or Sao Tome and Principe.
evidence: Summary of country-specific statistical tests

claim: Almost half of phone owners are under 30 years old.
source: In all age classes, a high proportion of individuals own mobile phones; almost half of phone owners are under 30 years old.
evidence: Observation from age-stratified analysis

claim: For women aged 18-30 years old, they are more likely to own a smartphone than a basic phone.
source: For women, 18–30 year olds (and for men, 18–35 year olds) are more likely to own an SP than a BP
evidence: Pattern observed in age and gender-stratified analysis

claim: For men aged 18-35 years old, they are more likely to own a smartphone than a basic phone.
source: For women, 18–30 year olds (and for men, 18–35 year olds) are more likely to own an SP than a BP
evidence: Pattern observed in age and gender-stratified analysis

claim: In all age classes, a greater proportion of men than women own mobile phones.
source: In all age classes, a greater proportion of men than women own mobile phones
evidence: Pattern observed in age and gender-stratified analysis

claim: The gender inequity in mobile phone ownership is accentuated for smartphones.
source: this gender inequity in ownership is accentuated for SPs.
evidence: Comparative observation from the analysis

claim: All odds ratios in the Bayesian multilevel logistic regression models for mobile phone ownership are significantly different from one in both bivariable and multivariable analysis.
source: All ORs are significantly different from one in both the bivariable and multivariable analysis.
evidence: Summary statement about statistical significance of model results

claim: The wealthiest individuals have approximately three times higher odds of owning mobile phones than the poorest individuals (aOR: 2.87, 95% HPD region: 2.53–3.27).
source: The probability of ownership decreases with the LPI; the wealthiest individuals have approximately three times higher odds of owning mobile phones than the poorest individuals (aOR: 2.87, 95% HPD region: 2.53–3.27).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis

claim: Country-specific effects are apparent for the inequity in ownership based on gender and urban/rural residency.
source: Country-specific effects are apparent for the inequity in ownership based on gender (Figure 4A) and urban/rural residency (Figure 4B)
evidence: Observation from multilevel model results shown in figures

claim: Men who do not live in close proximity to a health clinic had higher odds of smartphone ownership (aOR: 1.50, 95% HPD region: 1.30–1.72) than women who do not live in close proximity.
source: Men who do not live in close proximity to an HC had higher odds of SP ownership (aOR: 1.50, 95% HPD region: 1.30–1.72) than women who do not live in close proximity (1; the baseline category).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis with interaction effects

claim: Men in close proximity to a health clinic had even larger odds of owning a smartphone (aOR: 1.92, 95% HPD region: 1.63–2.26) than women in close proximity (aOR: 1.15, 95% HPD region: 1.03–1.30).
source: The gender difference is accentuated by proximity to an HC: men in close proximity to an HC had even larger odds of owning an SP (aOR: 1.92, 95% HPD region: 1.63–2.26) than women in close proximity (aOR: 1.15, 95% HPD region: 1.03–1.30).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis with interaction effects

claim: Ownership of smartphones among mobile phone owners is most likely in 18-30 year olds and decreases with age.
source: Ownership of SPs (amongst owners of mobile phones) is most likely in 18–30 year olds and decreases with age.
evidence: Pattern observed in age-stratified analysis

claim: The wealthiest individuals who own mobile phones are approximately three times more likely than the poorest individuals who own mobile phones to own smartphones (aOR: 2.86, 95% HPD region: 2.57–3.17).
source: The odds of ownership decrease with the LPI: the wealthiest individuals (who own mobile phones) are approximately three times more likely than the poorest individuals (who own mobile phones) to own SPs (aOR: 2.86, 95% HPD region: 2.57–3.17).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariable Bayesian analysis

claim: In many of the 33 countries, ownership of mobile phones is relatively high even amongst the poorest wealth classes for both basic phones and smartphones.
source: Notably, in many of the 33 countries, ownership of mobile phones is relatively high even amongst the poorest of the wealth classes; this holds true for both BPs and, more surprisingly, SPs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observation from wealth-stratified analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Women may be less likely than men to own mobile phones due to receiving less education, higher levels of poverty, and cultural norms of patriarchy.
source: Women may be less likely than men to own mobile phones due to receiving less education (which results in lower levels of literacy and digital literacy), higher levels of poverty, and cultural norms of patriarchy that prevent female empowerment and reduce the agency of women (GSMA, 2022; LeFevre et al., 2020; Marron et al., 2020; Paradigm Initiative, 2020; Porter et al., 2020).
evidence: Explanation supported by citations to previous research

claim: The rural population may be less likely than urban residents to own mobile phones due to fewer years of schooling, lower levels of literacy and digital literacy, and higher levels of poverty.
source: The rural population may be less likely than urban residents to own mobile phones due to many of the same factors (fewer years of schooling, lower levels of literacy and digital literacy, and higher levels of poverty; GSMA, 2020; Houngbonon et al., 2021; Wesolowski et al., 2012).
evidence: Explanation supported by citations to previous research

claim: The main driver of urban-rural inequality in mobile phone ownership may be that there is less infrastructure in rural areas than in urban areas.
source: However, the main driver of the inequality may be that there is less infrastructure in rural areas than in urban areas (Krönke, 2020; Krönke et al., 2022); rural areas have lower cell coverage, a less reliable source of electricity, and often lack high-speed broadband (Houngbonon et al., 2021).
evidence: Explanation supported by citations to previous research

claim: Over the past few years in Africa, smartphones have increasingly become an essential tool for improving an individual's livelihood and daily affairs.
source: This may be explained by the fact that, over the past few years in Africa, SPs have increasingly become an essential tool for improving an individuals' livelihood and daily affairs (Alliance for Affordable Internet, 2020; World Health Organization, 2021b).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to reports

claim: Smartphones are used to access government services and healthcare, for agricultural purposes, commerce, education, expanding employment opportunities, promoting entrepreneurialism, and electronic money transfer.
source: SPs are used to access government services and healthcare (e.g. to register for COVID-19 vaccination), for agricultural purposes, commerce, education, expanding employment opportunities, promoting entrepreneurialism, and electronic money transfer (Alliance for Affordable Internet, 2020; Etzo and Collender, 2010; Marsh et al., 2020; Porter et al., 2018; Poushter and Oates, 2015; Quandt et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2021b).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: Some of the poorest individuals may own smartphones due to their participation in the national Village Phone Program.
source: Additionally, some of the poorest individuals may own SPs due to their participation in the national Village Phone Program (Futch and McIntosh, 2009), which operates in multiple African countries such as Nigeria, Uganda, and Rwanda.
evidence: Explanation supported by citation to previous research

claim: The Village Phone Program operates in multiple African countries such as Nigeria, Uganda, and Rwanda.
source: which operates in multiple African countries such as Nigeria, Uganda, and Rwanda.
evidence: Statement about the geographic scope of a program

claim: In the Village Phone Program, an individual subscribes by taking a loan and buying a smartphone, then is trained on how to operate it and make a profit by charging others to use it.
source: An individual subscribes to the program by taking a loan and buying an SP; they are then trained on how to operate the SP and to make a profit by charging others to use it.
evidence: Description of how a program operates

claim: Many of the inequalities in mobile phone ownership are the same inequalities that exist in accessing healthcare and health-related information.
source: Many of the inequalities that we have found exist in the ownership of mobile phones are the same inequalities that exist in accessing healthcare and health-related information.
evidence: Comparative observation linking findings to broader context

claim: Individuals living in rural areas have the greatest difficulty in accessing healthcare and health-related information due to the geographic distribution of healthcare facilities.
source: Individuals living in rural areas – due to the geographic distribution of healthcare facilities – have the greatest difficulty in accessing healthcare and health-related information (Palk et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2021a)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: The most vulnerable members of society (women, children, the elderly, and those living in poverty) have the greatest difficulty in accessing healthcare and health-related information.
source: Similarly, the most vulnerable members of society (women, children, the elderly, and those living in poverty) have the greatest difficulty in accessing healthcare and health-related information
evidence: Statement about healthcare access disparities

claim: The most vulnerable members of society are often the most in need of healthcare.
source: Notably, these vulnerable members of society are often the most in need of healthcare, e.g., women are in need of healthcare personnel for assistance with childbirth and antenatal care, and children are in need of protection against malaria and vaccination against childhood diseases.
evidence: Statement about healthcare needs with examples

claim: mHealth approaches are currently being used at a small-scale to diagnose and treat over a dozen diseases and health conditions in Africa.
source: mHealth approaches are currently being used, at a small-scale, to diagnose and treat over a dozen diseases and health conditions in Africa (Holst et al., 2020; Manby et al., 2022; Onukwugha et al., 2022; Osei et al., 2021; Wood et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to recent studies

claim: Treatment of infectious diseases of relatively long duration, such as tuberculosis and HIV, has received the most attention in mHealth interventions.
source: Treatment of infectious diseases of relatively long duration, such as tuberculosis and HIV, has received the most attention (Manby et al., 2022; Maraba et al., 2018; Nwaozuru et al., 2021; Osei et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: mHealth interventions are being explored for non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and conditions such as alcohol consumption and hearing loss.
source: However, mHealth interventions are also being explored for non-communicable diseases, such as diabetes (Dike et al., 2021), cancer (Mutebi et al., 2020), and conditions such as alcohol consumption (Suleman et al., 2021) and hearing loss (Bhamjee et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Many pilot mHealth interventions have been launched throughout Africa to manage Ebola, maternal health, and various childhood ailments.
source: Throughout Africa, many pilot mHealth interventions have been launched to manage Ebola (Tom-Aba et al., 2018), maternal health (Ag Ahmed et al., 2017; Mildon and Sellen, 2019; Onukwugha et al., 2022), and various childhood ailments (Mahmood et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: The majority of mHealth interventions implemented in Africa have focused on using SMS/texting to improve treatment adherence and patient retention.
source: To date, the majority of mHealth interventions that have been implemented in Africa have focused on using SMS/texting to improve treatment adherence and patient retention (Kruse et al., 2019; Manby et al., 2022; Odukoya et al., 2021)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: SMS/texting-based mHealth interventions only require access to basic phones.
source: notably, such interventions only require access to BPs.
evidence: Statement about technical requirements

claim: Weekly text messaging to HIV patients that are literate (and voice-enabled systems for illiterate patients) have substantially improved adherence to medication and increased retention in care.
source: Studies of these interventions have shown that weekly text messaging to HIV patients that are literate (and voice-enabled systems for illiterate patients) have substantially improved adherence to medication and increased retention in care.
evidence: Statement about intervention effectiveness based on previous studies

claim: mHealth approaches in Africa are being investigated for increasing access to medical education and training for health workers.
source: mHealth approaches in Africa are currently being investigated for their utility in increasing access to medical education and training for health workers (Anstey Watkins et al., 2018)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth approaches are being investigated as a platform to support nurses and midwives.
source: as a platform to support nurses and midwives (Nigussie et al., 2021)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth approaches are being investigated to improve men's access to HIV self-testing.
source: to improve men's access to HIV self-testing (van Heerden et al., 2017)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: mHealth approaches are being investigated for public health messaging, disease surveillance, symptom monitoring, epidemic outbreak tracking, and to aid vaccination campaigns.
source: public health messaging (Downs et al., 2019), disease surveillance (Brinkel et al., 2014; Wood et al., 2019), symptom monitoring (Lai et al., 2019; Wood et al., 2019), epidemic outbreak tracking (Singh et al., 2019), and to aid vaccination campaigns (e.g. for COVID-19; Fischer et al., 2021; Oliver-Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: Several systematic reviews have concluded that some (but not all) mHealth programs that have been initiated have a positive impact on health behaviors and outcomes, especially in rural and remote communities.
source: Several systematic reviews have concluded that some (but not all) of the mHealth programs that have been initiated have a positive impact on health behaviors and outcomes, especially in rural and remote communities (Ag Ahmed et al., 2017; Mbuthia et al., 2019; Mildon and Sellen, 2019; Oliver-Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to systematic reviews

claim: mHealth interventions have the potential to increase the quality, reduce the cost, and extend the reach of healthcare.
source: mHealth interventions have the potential to increase the quality, reduce the cost, and extend the reach of healthcare (Holst et al., 2020; Manby et al., 2022; Onukwugha et al., 2022; Osei et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: Those who are most in need of mHealth interventions are those in rural areas who do not live in close proximity to a health clinic.
source: Those who are most in need of mHealth interventions are those in rural areas who do not live in close proximity to an HC
evidence: Inference based on healthcare access patterns

claim: Individuals in rural areas who do not live in close proximity to a health clinic are currently far less likely to own mobile phones than individuals in urban areas who live in close proximity to a health clinic.
source: However, our results show that these individuals are currently far less likely to own mobile phones than individuals who may have less need of mHealth interventions, i.e., individuals in urban areas who live in close proximity to an HC.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings

claim: mHealth interventions need to be designed to take age, geographic variation, and inequities based on gender, urban/rural residency and wealth in ownership of basic phones and smartphones into consideration.
source: Notably, our results demonstrate that mHealth interventions need to be designed to take age, geographic variation, and inequities (based on gender, urban/rural residency and wealth) in ownership of BPs and SPs into consideration.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings

claim: It will be critical to consider the impact of education and low levels of literacy on the ownership and usage of mobile phones and on the design of mHealth interventions.
source: Previous studies have shown that it will also be critical to consider the impact of education and low levels of literacy on the ownership and usage of mobile phones and hence on the design of mHealth interventions (Krönke, 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research

claim: Due to current levels of mobile phone ownership, it may only be possible to scale up mHealth interventions in a few countries but not in the vast majority of the 33 countries analyzed.
source: Our results suggest that, due to current levels of mobile phone ownership, it may only be possible to scale up mHealth interventions in a few countries (e.g. Botswana; United Nations, 2021), but not in the vast majority of the 33 countries that we have analyzed.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings

claim: Smartphones are not yet widely used in many African countries.
source: SPs are not yet widely used in many African countries
evidence: Observation from the study findings

claim: In the foreseeable future, high-tech mHealth interventions that require smartphones will be hard to implement in the low-ownership countries identified in the analyses.
source: hence in the foreseeable future, high-tech mHealth interventions that require SPs (and regular access to the internet), rather than lower-tech interventions that only require BPs, will be hard to implement in the low-ownership countries that we have identified in our analyses.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study findings

claim: Before the promise of mHealth interventions can be reached in Africa, there is a need for a 'digital transformation' to occur throughout the continent.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that before the promise of mHealth interventions can be reached in Africa, there is a need for a 'digital transformation' to occur throughout the continent.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study findings
